title: One prompt, three shapes
spec: M04 · the same TypeScript request into all three CLIs
intro: The identical sentence goes into Claude Code, Gemini CLI and Copilot CLI. Two of them return a file. The third returns a shell command — and that is the answer it was built to give. Four steps, then the scorecard.

provenance.source: the three arms are this module's own captured tool transcripts, replayed step by step; the Copilot menu is reproduced verbatim from the page

foot: Every line here is on this page already — scroll back to #claude-output-1, #gemini-output-1 and the panel above to read the full files.

steps.title: The prompt, sent verbatim to three tools
narrative: One sentence, copied character-for-character into three terminals. No follow-up, no clarification, no CLAUDE.md or GEMINI.md steering — because the moment you tune the prompt per tool you are comparing your prompts, not the tools.

Fix the marking scheme before you look at any output. Correctness, TypeScript quality, error handling, test-readiness, conciseness. Write the columns down now so you cannot quietly move the goalposts once you have a favourite.
One column is going to come back empty, and the interesting question is not which — it is whether an empty column is a failure or a category error.

steps.title: Claude Code — 52 lines that throw
narrative: Claude Code writes a file. FetchError extends Error and carries status and url; fetchWithRetry<T> is generic over the response shape, so callers get typing without a cast. Backoff is baseDelayMs * 2 ** attempt with ±25% jitter.

The judgement call worth noticing is the 4xx/5xx split. A 404 is not going to become a 200 on the third attempt, so it throws immediately; a 500 is retried. That is a decision about your API's semantics, made without being asked.

Where it is thin: there is no timeout. A socket that opens and then never answers will sit there past every retry, because fetch without an AbortController has no deadline. And 429 — rate limiting, the single most common retriable status in practice — falls under 4xx and is therefore not retried. Hold both of those against the next arm.
steps.claudeSays: Writes one file, exports the error class, throws on failure. 52 lines, WHAT/WHY/GOTCHA comments per block.

terminal.text:
Writing a generic wrapper. 5xx and network errors retry with

state.label: Claude Code output · the shape of the contract

before.title: THE SIGNATURE — errors leave through throw

lines: // 4xx: do not retry — the request itself is malformed
view.note: Promise<T> — the happy path returns the data itself, so a caller writes const u = await fetchWithRetry<User>(url) and wraps it in try/catch. That is the TypeScript convention, and expect(...).rejects.toThrow(FetchError) is a one-line test. No timeout anywhere in the file.

steps.title: Gemini CLI — 68 lines that return
narrative: Gemini CLI also writes a file, and it fills exactly the two holes the previous arm left. AbortController gives every attempt a 30-second deadline, and retryOnStatus: [429, 500, 502, 503, 504] puts rate limiting back in the retry set where it belongs. There is a maxDelay cap too, so attempt five does not sleep for a minute.

It pays for that with a different contract. ApiResponse<T> wraps every outcome — { data, error, attempts } — so nothing ever throws. Callers must remember to check .error, and a caller who forgets gets null data and no signal at all. In a try/catch codebase that is a foreign body; in a Go-flavoured, errors-as-values codebase it is exactly right.

16 more lines, and every one of them buys something. "More verbose" and "more configurable" are the same fact viewed from two directions — which one you call it depends on whether you needed the configuration.
steps.claudeSays: Writes one file, returns a wrapper type, never throws. 68 lines, timeout and status list configurable.

state.label: two working files, two different contracts

lines: export async function fetchWithRetry<T>(url, options): Promise<T>
// no timeout — a hung socket outlives all 4 attempts
// 429 is 4xx, so rate limits are never retried
export async function fetchUserData<T>(url, options, config): Promise<ApiResponse<T>>
// nothing throws — a caller who forgets .error gets silent null
view.note: Both compile, both ship. The choice is a house-style choice: does a failed request raise, or does it return? Pick the one your existing codebase already does, because mixing the two is worse than either.

steps.title: Copilot CLI answers a different question — on purpose
narrative: The third arm never produces a .ts file. gh copilot suggest asks what kind of shell command you want, you pick generic shell command, and it hands back an npx ts-node -e invocation wrapping a stub with // stub — implement logic here inside it. Then it offers to copy the command to your clipboard.

Read that as a category error rather than a defeat. gh copilot suggest is a shell command translator: natural language in, one shell command out. Asking it for a typed retry helper is like asking a spell-checker for a plot. This module's own note is blunt about it — "This is not a weakness — it is intentional design."

Aim it at the job it was built for and it is the best of the three. gh copilot suggest "create a new TypeScript project with tsconfig and package.json" returns the exact incantation nobody remembers, first time, with no file to review. And GitHub Copilot in the editor writes TypeScript functions as well as anything here — that is a different product on a different surface, and this module compares CLIs only.

view.text: Two of these tools answered the question and one answered a different question well. Claude Code gives you the idiomatic file and leaves the timeout to you; Gemini CLI gives you the timeout and the 429 handling and asks you to adopt a wrapper type; gh copilot suggest gives you the shell line and never pretends to give you more. The scorecard in the next section is only fair if you read the last row too — a tool with an empty column is not losing a race it entered.
